To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the onset of extensive metallurgy in the Central Andes occurred ~2700 years BP, (2) the earliest evidence for extensive metallurgy is found in the Illimani ice cores, which is the first ice-core record of extensive metallurgy, and (3) this record provides the first complete history for the onset and evolution of metallurgy in the central Andes.
the earliest extensive copper metallurgic activities in the Andean Altipano occurred ~2700 years BP, during the Early Horizon Period.
the onset of large-scale copper metallurgy in South American prehistory was ~2700 years BP.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our ice-core data show that the onset of large-scale Cu metallurgy in the central Andean Altiplanos occurred ~2700 years BP and that this activity was already present during the early Chiripa and early Chavin cultures.
the onset of large-scale Cu metallurgy in the central Andes is dated to ~2700 years BP, which is in agreement with the onset of metallurgy in other parts of the world.
the onset of intensive copper smelting in the central Andes occurred around 2700 years BP, which is consistent with the archaeological record for the Chavin culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the onset of extensive metallurgy in the central Andes was much earlier than previously assumed.
the onset of extensive copper metallurgy is earlier than previously thought, and occurred during the Early Horizon ~2000–50 BC.

the Chiripa and the Chavin culture, both of which are considered the cradles of Andean metallurgy, were the first to produce large quantities of Cu, which was then transported over long distances, thus establishing a trade network in the Andes.
